White Paper Report
Northeastern University | Boston, MA
2025 ASNE PEP Competition
PEP Team
Jonah Jaffe: CEO and Co-Founder
Elizabeth Collins: Boat Project Lead
Evan Lin: Mechanical
Charlotte Stieve: Chief Safety Officer
Lily Miles: Electrical Lead
Neo Isak: Software
Nikolas Sanderson: Electrical
Elizabeth Carney: Electrical
Michelle Liu: Electrical
Mira Rieley: Mechanical and Chemical
Meera Patel: Mechanical and Chemical
Sam Elkerton: Electrical and Software
David Mitchell: Mechanical
Maya Krattli: Mechanical and Chemical
Craft: Usain Boat
1Background

Marine electrical propulsion systems have been of increasing interest as concern
for the environmental impact of the shipping, and transportation industries grows [1].
Further, electrification could allow for en route recharging that could extend the range of
vessels and increase cost efficiency [2]. With advances in the energy density and reliability
of battery technology, a reality where fully electric marine vessels are a significant portion
of the shipping, transportation and even the tourism industries seems highly feasible.
With electric propulsion, there are a few key factors to consider. The hull design
factors from any other medium of ship design still apply, with certain profiles providing
more efficiency, stability and ability to handle vibrations. The density of water is 1000
times larger than that of air and since drag is proportional to fluid density, efficient boat
hulls focus on optimizing their designs around minimizing water drag in a few ways. The
first is that hulls are designed such that the portion in contact with the water cuts through
it. This can be done with shapes with low drag coefficients (Figure 1) [3].
Figure 1: Drag coefficients of different shapes Equation 1: The equation for drag
Additionally, some boats focus on minimizing the part of the hull that is in the
water using a hydrofoil or a hydroplane to generate lift. Many of the world’s fastest boats
do this, but this is a high risk, high reward strategy. If you do not generate the requisite lift
for planing or foiling, you risk having a part of a boat with a high drag coefficient being in
the water. We weighed this risk heavily when considering the hull shape for our vessel.
At NUWave, we come from an underwater robotics background. We’re used to
waterproofing everything for a depth of 15 meters and focusing on every little detail
because one mistake can be costly. The team applies this philosophy to the creation of
our surface vessels. We aim to create a “bulletproof boat”, a vehicle that will work, not
just in optimal conditions, but when faced with the harsh realities of ocean environments.
You can see this in every aspect of our design, from redundancy in our hull for increased
flotation, to choosing electronic parts with extra capacity to handle current draw spikes.
Design and Analysis
Propeller and Motor
When choosing a motor to optimize the efficiency of the electric propulsion
system, the goal was to balance the factors of torque and RPM (rotations per minute).
RPM is often optimized around a different factor of kV or RPM per volt because it allows
you to draw a direct correlation between power storage requirements and thrust output.
There are a few key factors to consider with this approach though. Primarily kV ratings can
be specified for different input amperages at the same voltage range. This was the case
when comparing our two top motor choices, the Leopard 56110, and the TP Power 5870.
Each of these motors have a variant that takes 36 volts, something that would work with
our planned power storage system, and the TP Power 5870 offered a greater kV of 1100
compared to the Leopard 56110’s.
2kV Voltage Nominal Power RPM per kW

Leopard 56110 950 36V 7560W 125.66
TP Power 5870 1100 36V 9000W 122.22
Table 1: Motor efficiency comparisons
As seen in the table above, while the TP Power 5870 offers a higher kV, it is in fact
less efficient for the amount of power given than the Leopard 56110, making the Leopard
56110 the power optimal choice. Lower kV motors are often ideal when you want higher
torque, as spinning slower allows for greater propeller diameters without overheating
electronics. The initially high torque of these two motors is why they were selected as
good candidates in the first place in the first place. Many aerial drone motors have better
kVs than our selected choices, but due to their lack of torque, they cannot effectively push
water without slowing down significantly or cavitating. The Leopard 56110 motor is
designed to be an inboard motor and as such has the requisite torque (Figure 2).
Figure 2: ZTW Seal 300A ESC and the Leopard 56110 motor
DC brushless motors require electronic speed controllers (ESCs) to provide the
3-phase current required for driving the motor. ESCs are a common failure point of
electric propulsion systems as they heat up the fastest of any part and contain sensitive
electronics that can fail if the motor overdraws. The ZTW Seal 300A ESC gave us a factor
of safety of 1.4 over our current limit of 210A, all while coming with a pre-installed cooling
jacket for heat dissipation (Figure 2). Further, the ZTW Seal is waterproof allowing us to
have confidence in it even in the case of a potentially dangerous leak.
Another important potential failure point to consider is the drive shaft. In using the
torque calculations and our diameter of 6.35mm, we experience a shear force of 37.8MPa.
A 304 stainless steel drive shaft was chosen for its shear force of 386MPa [4]. This gives a
factor of safety of 10.21. The shear force experienced by the motor mount and screws is
also considered (Figure 3)

Table 2: The shear force experienced by our motor mounting bracket and screws
When choosing a propeller manufacturer, Octura propellers [5] stood out as a
reputable source with a wide variety of options to allow us to find an exact fit for our
needs. In selecting propellers, our goal was to balance efficiency with thrust output. The
industry recommendation is a minimum of 60mm [6] for a boat of our size and that left us
with the Octura X-series. Of the X-series, there are propellers with two to three blades.
Two-bladed propellers result in higher efficiency, reduced loads on electronics, and less
drag [7]. Alternatively, three-bladed propellers provide greater thrust and less vibration,
which is ideal for races with heavy payloads. Indeterminate of blade count, the pitch
determines the amount of forward movement the boat is able to move with each rotation.
Higher pitches result in faster top speeds at the cost of more load on the motor [8]. Lower
pitches are slower, but are more ideal for payloads and reducing the load on the motor
and therefore heat generation.
Given those constraints, we narrowed down our search to the following options:
Propeller Diameter (mm) Pitch (in) Shaft Size (in) Material # Blades
Octura X467 67 3.696 1/4 BC 2
Octura X470 70 3.864 1/4 BC 2
Octura X470/3 70 3.864 1/4 BC 3
Octura X472 72 3.967 1/4 BC 2
Octura X482 82 4.508 1/4 BC 2
Table 3: Propeller comparison payload
While the X482 is too large for the high RPMs of our motor and would likely lead to
overheating of the electronics, the other options were close enough that the X470 and
X470/3 were purchased for testing. Selecting this middle-ground would allow the team to
specify slightly larger or smaller dimensions depending on testing results, which are
discussed in our propeller and propulsion system fabrication section.
4Hull

A mid-rise V-shaped monohull was chosen for the design of the hull of Usain Boat.
The V-shape aspect allows the vehicle to withstand the somewhat choppy waters that are
typically seen in the race location while still maintaining a low draft for easier planing
speeds and reduced drag. The monohull cockpit provided ample room to house all
electronics plus the additional 30-60 lb payload.
The monohull design took inspiration from skiffs, sonars, and the Provincetown I
Ferry, which are all designed for handling heavy payloads while maintaining stability
against heavy winds and rapid waters. For the initial design, the original Provincetown I
Ferry lines plan, drafted by Gilbert Associates Inc. was studied for basic overall length,
beam, chine, and draft dimensions (Figure 4).
Figure 4: The Lines Plans for the Provincetown I Ferry
While the Provincetown I Ferry design provided a good starting point for the
design of Usain Boat, many changes needed to be made to iteratively improve its
dimensions and performance for the competition. An initial concern the team needed to
address was our ability to transport the boat in and out of our workspace. This
constrained the dimensions to ensure the vehicle could fit in elevators, tight doorways,
and an SUV trunk. As such, the overall length of the boat could not exceed six feet
inclusive of the propulsion system. Furthermore, in order to reduce wet drag, the vehicle
needed to be narrow and have a shallow draft, while still displacing enough water to carry
the payload and electronics. In order to find the ideal shape for the boat based on these
constraints, several calculations and simulations were performed.
First, a lines plan was designed in FREE!Ship, an open source software commonly
used within industry. This lines plane took into account the maximum length of the boat, a
10-20 degree variable deadrise, and a maximum width of no more than 24” to remain
under the CNC machining limitations.
Figure 5: An initial CAD model of Usain Boat
5The lines plan was then imported to SolidWorks to develop a 3D model for volume

analysis at waterlines of 4 and 4.5 inches from the bottom of the hull and eventual CNC
machining (Figure 5) . The volumes were substituted into the buoyancy force equation
shown below:

The design was scaled down and 3D printed to observe potential fiberglassing
issues, center of buoyancies, and machining issues. After 17 design iterations, two
designs were finalized that fit the dimension and calculation specifications; however, one
had a rounded bottom while the other had a chine. Although rounded bottoms are
optimal for displacement hulls, they are less stable and harder to fiberglass without
multiple relief cuts. Thus, the chine design was finalized upon as seen in the lines plan
below (Figure 6).
Figure 6: Lines Plan for the final boat design
All of the important dimensions of the boat were organized into the following table:
Table 4: Important dimension calculations for Usain Boat
6Additionally, the design was imported into Ansys to run a computational fluid

dynamic (CFD) analysis on the drag force on the hull (Figure 7). The final results estimated
the drag force to be approximately 60N at 10 mph under ideal conditions; however, the
final drag force is expected to be higher than 60N due to fabrication imperfections,
unpredictable environmental forces, and Ansys Fluent’s limitation to static bodies.
Figure 7: Ansys Simulation of drag force on the hull
Once the design of the boat was finalized, the boat material needed to be
determined. Wood, metal, and carbon fiber are all common in boat hull construction,
however, fiberglass was chosen due to it being cost effective, high strength, moldable,
and lightweight. A foam base would be used to carve out the shape, allowing for
relatively easy edits for custom sized compartments for electronics and payloads while
maintaining a light weight, high buoyancy, and internal structural support.
Overview of Build and Fabrication Processes
Hull Fabrication
In order to become familiar with the process of building a boat hull from epoxy, a
scaled down version of the craft was first constructed (Figure 8). This prototype of Usain
Boat was first created using a combination of 3D printed parts for either end of the boat
and foam that was cut using a hot wire cutter for the center. It originally aimed to be
constructed fully out of foam, however there were difficulties in accurately cutting out the
curve of the V-shape at the bow. The 3D printed parts and foam center were then covered
in fiberglass, which then was covered in epoxy to create the hull.
Figure 8: First trial of hull creation
Based on the difficulties faced with cutting the foam for this smaller version of the
vehicle, and the impracticability of 3D printing the base of our hull, it was decided that
the foam for the shape of the hull would be cut out using a CNC machine (Figure 9).
Multiple layers of foam were stacked and glued together, then cut into the shape of a
mid-rise V-hull.
7Figure 9: The boat hull after being cut out on the CNC machine

After being cut out, the sides of the craft had to be sanded down to create a
smooth surface that the fiberglass and epoxy could be shaped around. Once this was
completed fiberglass strips were placed on the foam mold, then covered in a thin layer of
epoxy to dry. This process was performed outside, and with proper personal protective
equipment to keep all involved safe from the epoxy and fiberglass (Figure 10).
Figure 10: Putting the fiberglass and epoxy on the foam boat mold (15°F)
Figure 11: Usain Boat after being trimmed and painted
Multiple layers of fiberglass and epoxy were put on to reinforce the hull of the
boat, with special care taken around the bow and stern where the boat would experience
the most force. Once the epoxy was fully dried, the edges had excess pooling of epoxy.
The edges were trimmed with an angle grinder before proceeding. The bottom of the
boat was then painted and holes were drilled into the stern for the propeller and rudders
(Figure 11). While the paint was drying, a cradle was built to hold the boat in an upright
position while working on the deck.
8Figure 12: Fiberglassing the deck, adding a space for the tow rope, and foam cutting the motor bay

The next steps were to begin fiberglassing the top of the boat, to create
compartments to house the electronics within the boat, and to add an attachment point
for a tow rope (Figure 12). By this point it had been decided that the foam mold of the
hull was going to stay inside of the fiberglass and epoxy shell, ensuring stability of the
craft, and providing extra protection from water entering the vehicle. Further, this allowed
for the compartments of our electronics to be cut directly into this foam (Figure 13). These
compartments were cut using a hot wire cutter, slowly cutting away strips of foam until the
compartment was the proper depth and width. A piece of wood was also added for
stability reasons after cutting away the foam.
Figure 13: Usain Boat after having the electronics compartments cut out
After cutting out these compartments, they were covered in a layer of fiberglass
and epoxy as well, and watertight lids for the compartments were fitted into the boat.
Electronics were then placed inside, and the rest of the boat was painted.
Propeller and Propulsion System
Our team’s experience with underwater robotics, a field where focusing on every
minor detail is critical, was something we were able to apply to the fabrication of our
propulsion system. We took extra care to ensure that both of our propellers were
sharpened and balanced to increase efficiency and reduce vibration. We also made sure
to fill our stuffing tube with marine grease to ensure that no water would leak in and to
minimize friction.
9Figure 14: The Octura X470/2 (left) and X470/3 (right)

In terms of testing the two bladed and three bladed propeller, the team came to
the conclusion that the three bladed X470’s superior thrust outweighed the efficiency
benefits generated from the two bladed propeller (Figure 14). This was largely because
we had the battery capacity for the 5 mile race from 2024, making the 2 mile race easily
feasible. The propellers also both didn’t cavitate, implying that the diameter and pitch of
the propeller was sufficiently close to optimal for creating thrust efficiently without
rotating too fast and pushing air.
Figure 15: The propeller ventilation (left) and the propeller stable after adjustments were made (right)
In testing propellers, the team also focused on drive shaft angle for two reasons.
Firstly, a downward angled drive shaft can provide some upward force that pushes more
of the hull out of the water, reducing drag. Additionally, the drive shaft not being deep
enough underwater would make it easier for air to be sucked under the surface and cause
ventilation (Figure 15). We determined the optimal angle through experimental testing
and bent our stuffing tube to the correct angle.
The final modification considered was a gearbox or belt drive. These options would
trade off RPM for torque while maintaining motor efficiency. The team decided on a direct
drive system as it significantly reduced the number of failure points, a conscious decision
to sacrifice some performance benefits for reliability, something befitting of our design
principles. RPM limiting is still maintainable in the software of the system.
The entire propulsion system of the craft can be seen laid out below (Figure 16).
Figure 16: Usain Boat’s Electric Propulsion System
10Power Storage

In terms of batteries, the vehicle is powered by 2 MaxAmps Lithium 8s 20000mAh
Li-Ion batteries configured in parallel (Figure 17). These batteries are able to output a
continuous 100 amps each, however running these batteries in parallel allows for the
output of the amperage to be doubled, which in turn allows for more speed for Usain
Boat. Additionally, these batteries boast an energy density that is unrivaled by other
market options. At 250 Wh/kg, they outperform almost all other batteries in energy
density, especially in the 8S range.
Figure 17: MaxAmps Lithium ion batteries
There are a few 6s options with up to 300 Wh/kg, but they are all LiPo batteries
which are significantly less safe than Lion batteries, with a much higher likelihood of
combusting if improperly used. While safer than LiPo batteries to begin with, the
MaxAmps Lithium batteries also have automatic internal cell balancing to prevent an
individual cell from getting over drained and failing before the battery is too low.
Figure 18: Marine access hatch
The batteries for the craft are stored in the center of the boat, with one on each
side for proper weight distribution. They are protected by a watertight lid, as well as
multiple layers of foam, and are velcroed down to an acrylic plate within the vehicle
(Figure 18).
Powertrain
In developing a power system, we wanted to separate our high power systems
from our sensing and controls suite for noise and safety reasons. Our high power safety
shutoff is 36V volt contactor that is controlled by a relay. To power our lower voltage
electronics, we use a 14S power conversion module. Using a 14S power module gives us
a significant factor of safety to handle power spikes, something we needed as last year we
blew a 10S power conversion module. The power diagram for the vehicle can be seen
below (Figure 19).
11Figure 19: High power systems and power conversion. Note that the nominal voltage of the system is 28.8V,

but it gets as high as 33V on full charge
For propulsion and steering, we use the aforementioned ZTW Seal 300A ESC and
Leopard 56110 on our 28.8V line, and we run our steering servos with 8.4V. They give
70kg of torque each and are waterproof, providing sufficient reliability (Figure 21).
Figure 20: Our propulsion and steering powertrain
Payload
With the introduction of a variable payload into this year’s competition, many
design decisions were made to adapt to this new format. To be as competitively viable as
possible, it was decided to make a payload flexible hull design for a pretty simple reason:
it gave the team the most paths to victory. In the event that the competition was filled
with fast, but light, 30lb payload boats, we could go light to keep pace with them. On the
other hand, if there is one exceptionally fast 30lb boat, but the rest are much slower, a
middling-speed 60lb payload boat can use its 5 point bonus to overtake the first place
team with a second place run time. As for our actual payload, we used steel shot balls in
shooting bags as they were maulable and adjustable to our needs (Figure 21).
Figure 21: Our payload bags (left) and our payload paths to the podium (right)
12Control System

Figure 22: The control and communications signals
The control system of the craft consists of a Pixhawk controller, a common flight
controller for RC drones and aircraft. We use the ArduRover firmware to configure our
pixhawk for use on Usain Boat. The flight controller has a built-in IMU. With an additional
GPS and current sensor we are able to monitor key facets of our craft. A Dragonlink RC
two-way radio system is used to control the vessel, and transmit telemetry data, such as
GPS location, current speed, and battery current draw and voltage to the pilot (Figure 22).
Figure 23: The Dragonlink RC Radio and Taranis controller
The Dragonlink system boasts a 50 km range, far more than is needed for the 2
mile race. For its price point, it is potentially the strongest commercial radio on the market
(Figure 23). Since the boat sits low in the water, there are concerns about Fresnel Zone
clearance. To alleviate that concern, Usain Boat’s receiver antenna is high up on the boat.
This combined with the strength of the transmitter provides a reliable solution against
obstructions and allows confidence in the performance of the craft’s radio.
Figure 24: The CAD and resulting 3D print of one of the rudders
13Since Usain Boat is equipped with only a single propeller, a separate rudder system

was created to steer the craft. This system adds a rudder on either side of the propeller
and these rudders are attached to servos that can be controlled with our Taranis controller
over a Dragonlink radio connection to turn the vehicle. The rudders were designed in
Solidworks, then 3D printed before being attached to our boat (Figure 24).
Risk
When designing a Usain Boat, it was important to take into account the risks
associated with the different parts of the craft. Usain Boat only has a singular propeller,
which poses complications in terms of turning the vehicle, ensuring there is enough
power from the singular propeller to drive the boat forward with a 30-60 pound payload,
and presents the risk of not having any propulsion should the propeller fail. In order to
account for these risks, proper protocols and additions to the craft have been put into
place. To handle the issue of steering a rudder system has been attached to the back of
the craft, allowing it to turn. Our team also makes sure to keep the propeller clear, both to
keep themselves safe and not cause damage to the propeller. There was also proper
research done to ensure the motor met the required specifications to provide the
propeller with enough power to move the craft, even while operating with a payload.
The motor of Usain Boat is connected to the propeller using a flexible shaft. This
flexible shaft is susceptible to unwinding if mishandled, so care is always taken whenever
attaching the motor and the propeller or when working with the shaft. In addition to this,
care and proper precautions are taken when working with the batteries that provide
power to the vehicle. The boat operates on Lithium ion batteries, which are safer than
LiPo batteries, but still pose risks. When the batteries are not in use, they are stored in a
flammables bag or in a flammables cabinet (Figure 25), and it is ensured that they are
charged properly to avoid damaging the batteries and increasing their risk of harm. There
is also always sand available in our lab space, in case a fire were to occur.
Figure 25: Lithium Ion Battery Bag Figure 26: Contactor Kill Switch
The team works with fiberglass and epoxy often, using them to fabricate the hull of
the vehicle, and can be exposed to harmful chemicals when working with these materials
as well as when participating in activities such as foam cutting. In order to minimize the
risk when working with these materials, it is ensured that proper protective equipment,
including gloves, masks, goggles, and respirators are worn. It is also ensured that these
materials are utilized correctly and safely. For example, we made sure that there was no
loose fiberglass on the hull of the boat and that all of the epoxy had cured correctly.
To account for any risks that could occur during the race, the craft has a contactor
kill switch installed, in addition to a physical kill switch, that allows Usain Boat to be shut
down remotely (Figure 26). That means if any issue is to occur during the race, the vehicle
can quickly and safely be shut down to minimize any potential hazards.
14Conclusion

Usain Boat is the result of well over 1000 hours of work from our dedicated team at
NUWave. It’s designed to be a “bulletproof boat,” capable of running reliably even in
adverse circumstances. It is equipped to operate at either the 30lb or 60lb payload
weight in order to optimize to competition circumstances, and it features an entirely new
propulsion system from last year’s design. It boasts a wide variety of safety features from
contactors to waterproof hatches to create a secure craft.
When considering future directions, the team is considering adding a second
propeller to both double the thrust and replace the rudder with a differential thrust
turning system for sharper corners. Our software system also enables improvement
through autonomy strategies like waypoint following and raceline optimization.

3-phase current required for driving the motor. ESCs are a common failure point of
electric propulsion systems as they heat up the fastest of any part and contain sensitive
electronics that can fail if the motor overdraws. The ZTW Seal 300A ESC gave us a factor
of safety of 1.4 over our current limit of 210A, all while coming with a pre-installed cooling
jacket for heat dissipation (Figure 2). Further, the ZTW Seal is waterproof allowing us to
have confidence in it even in the case of a potentially dangerous leak.
Another important potential failure point to consider is the drive shaft. In using the
torque calculations and our diameter of 6.35mm, we experience a shear force of 37.8MPa.
A 304 stainless steel drive shaft was chosen for its shear force of 386MPa [4]. This gives a
factor of safety of 10.21. The shear force experienced by the motor mount and screws is
also considered (Figure 3)

When choosing a propeller manufacturer, Octura propellers [5] stood out as a
reputable source with a wide variety of options to allow us to find an exact fit for our
needs. In selecting propellers, our goal was to balance efficiency with thrust output. The
industry recommendation is a minimum of 60mm [6] for a boat of our size and that left us
with the Octura X-series. Of the X-series, there are propellers with two to three blades.
Two-bladed propellers result in higher efficiency, reduced loads on electronics, and less
drag [7]. Alternatively, three-bladed propellers provide greater thrust and less vibration,
which is ideal for races with heavy payloads. Indeterminate of blade count, the pitch
determines the amount of forward movement the boat is able to move with each rotation.
Higher pitches result in faster top speeds at the cost of more load on the motor [8]. Lower
pitches are slower, but are more ideal for payloads and reducing the load on the motor
and therefore heat generation.

4Hull
A mid-rise V-shaped monohull was chosen for the design of the hull of Usain Boat.
The V-shape aspect allows the vehicle to withstand the somewhat choppy waters that are
typically seen in the race location while still maintaining a low draft for easier planing
speeds and reduced drag. The monohull cockpit provided ample room to house all
electronics plus the additional 30-60 lb payload.
The monohull design took inspiration from skiffs, sonars, and the Provincetown I
Ferry, which are all designed for handling heavy payloads while maintaining stability
against heavy winds and rapid waters. For the initial design, the original Provincetown I
Ferry lines plan, drafted by Gilbert Associates Inc. was studied for basic overall length,
beam, chine, and draft dimensions (Figure 4).
Figure 4: The Lines Plans for the Provincetown I Ferry
While the Provincetown I Ferry design provided a good starting point for the
design of Usain Boat, many changes needed to be made to iteratively improve its
dimensions and performance for the competition. An initial concern the team needed to
address was our ability to transport the boat in and out of our workspace. This
constrained the dimensions to ensure the vehicle could fit in elevators, tight doorways,
and an SUV trunk. As such, the overall length of the boat could not exceed six feet
inclusive of the propulsion system. Furthermore, in order to reduce wet drag, the vehicle
needed to be narrow and have a shallow draft, while still displacing enough water to carry
the payload and electronics. In order to find the ideal shape for the boat based on these
constraints, several calculations and simulations were performed.
First, a lines plan was designed in FREE!Ship, an open source software commonly
used within industry. This lines plane took into account the maximum length of the boat, a
10-20 degree variable deadrise, and a maximum width of no more than 24” to remain
under the CNC machining limitations.
Figure 5: An initial CAD model of Usain Boat

had a rounded bottom while the other had a chine. Although rounded bottoms are

Once the design of the boat was finalized, the boat material needed to be
determined. Wood, metal, and carbon fiber are all common in boat hull construction,
however, fiberglass was chosen due to it being cost effective, high strength, moldable,
and lightweight. A foam base would be used to carve out the shape, allowing for
relatively easy edits for custom sized compartments for electronics and payloads while
maintaining a light weight, high buoyancy, and internal structural support.
Overview of Build and Fabrication Processes
Hull Fabrication
In order to become familiar with the process of building a boat hull from epoxy, a
scaled down version of the craft was first constructed (Figure 8). This prototype of Usain
Boat was first created using a combination of 3D printed parts for either end of the boat
and foam that was cut using a hot wire cutter for the center. It originally aimed to be
constructed fully out of foam, however there were difficulties in accurately cutting out the
curve of the V-shape at the bow. The 3D printed parts and foam center were then covered
in fiberglass, which then was covered in epoxy to create the hull.
Figure 8: First trial of hull creation
Based on the difficulties faced with cutting the foam for this smaller version of the
vehicle, and the impracticability of 3D printing the base of our hull, it was decided that
the foam for the shape of the hull would be cut out using a CNC machine (Figure 9).
Multiple layers of foam were stacked and glued together, then cut into the shape of a
mid-rise V-hull.
7Figure 9: The boat hull after being cut out on the CNC machine
After being cut out, the sides of the craft had to be sanded down to create a
smooth surface that the fiberglass and epoxy could be shaped around. Once this was
completed fiberglass strips were placed on the foam mold, then covered in a thin layer of
epoxy to dry. This process was performed outside, and with proper personal protective
equipment to keep all involved safe from the epoxy and fiberglass (Figure 10).
Figure 10: Putting the fiberglass and epoxy on the foam boat mold (15°F)
Figure 11: Usain Boat after being trimmed and painted
Multiple layers of fiberglass and epoxy were put on to reinforce the hull of the
boat, with special care taken around the bow and stern where the boat would experience
the most force. Once the epoxy was fully dried, the edges had excess pooling of epoxy.
The edges were trimmed with an angle grinder before proceeding. The bottom of the
boat was then painted and holes were drilled into the stern for the propeller and rudders
(Figure 11). While the paint was drying, a cradle was built to hold the boat in an upright
position while working on the deck.
8Figure 12: Fiberglassing the deck, adding a space for the tow rope, and foam cutting the motor bay
The next steps were to begin fiberglassing the top of the boat, to create
compartments to house the electronics within the boat, and to add an attachment point
for a tow rope (Figure 12). By this point it had been decided that the foam mold of the
hull was going to stay inside of the fiberglass and epoxy shell, ensuring stability of the
craft, and providing extra protection from water entering the vehicle. Further, this allowed
for the compartments of our electronics to be cut directly into this foam (Figure 13). These
compartments were cut using a hot wire cutter, slowly cutting away strips of foam until the
compartment was the proper depth and width. A piece of wood was also added for
stability reasons after cutting away the foam.
Figure 13: Usain Boat after having the electronics compartments cut out
After cutting out these compartments, they were covered in a layer of fiberglass
and epoxy as well, and watertight lids for the compartments were fitted into the boat.
Electronics were then placed inside, and the rest of the boat was painted.
Propeller and Propulsion System
Our team’s experience with underwater robotics, a field where focusing on every
minor detail is critical, was something we were able to apply to the fabrication of our
propulsion system. We took extra care to ensure that both of our propellers were
sharpened and balanced to increase efficiency and reduce vibration. We also made sure
to fill our stuffing tube with marine grease to ensure that no water would leak in and to
minimize friction.
9Figure 14: The Octura X470/2 (left) and X470/3 (right)
In terms of testing the two bladed and three bladed propeller, the team came to
the conclusion that the three bladed X470’s superior thrust outweighed the efficiency
benefits generated from the two bladed propeller (Figure 14). This was largely because
we had the battery capacity for the 5 mile race from 2024, making the 2 mile race easily
feasible. The propellers also both didn’t cavitate, implying that the diameter and pitch of
the propeller was sufficiently close to optimal for creating thrust efficiently without
rotating too fast and pushing air.
Figure 15: The propeller ventilation (left) and the propeller stable after adjustments were made (right)
In testing propellers, the team also focused on drive shaft angle for two reasons.
Firstly, a downward angled drive shaft can provide some upward force that pushes more
of the hull out of the water, reducing drag. Additionally, the drive shaft not being deep
enough underwater would make it easier for air to be sucked under the surface and cause
ventilation (Figure 15). We determined the optimal angle through experimental testing
and bent our stuffing tube to the correct angle.
The final modification considered was a gearbox or belt drive. These options would
trade off RPM for torque while maintaining motor efficiency. The team decided on a direct
drive system as it significantly reduced the number of failure points, a conscious decision
to sacrifice some performance benefits for reliability, something befitting of our design
principles. RPM limiting is still maintainable in the software of the system.

Figure 16: Usain Boat’s Electric Propulsion System
10Power Storage
In terms of batteries, the vehicle is powered by 2 MaxAmps Lithium 8s 20000mAh
Li-Ion batteries configured in parallel (Figure 17). These batteries are able to output a
continuous 100 amps each, however running these batteries in parallel allows for the
output of the amperage to be doubled, which in turn allows for more speed for Usain
Boat. Additionally, these batteries boast an energy density that is unrivaled by other
market options. At 250 Wh/kg, they outperform almost all other batteries in energy
density, especially in the 8S range.
Figure 17: MaxAmps Lithium ion batteries
There are a few 6s options with up to 300 Wh/kg, but they are all LiPo batteries
which are significantly less safe than Lion batteries, with a much higher likelihood of
combusting if improperly used. While safer than LiPo batteries to begin with, the
MaxAmps Lithium batteries also have automatic internal cell balancing to prevent an
individual cell from getting over drained and failing before the battery is too low.
Figure 18: Marine access hatch
The batteries for the craft are stored in the center of the boat, with one on each
side for proper weight distribution. They are protected by a watertight lid, as well as
multiple layers of foam, and are velcroed down to an acrylic plate within the vehicle
(Figure 18).
Powertrain
In developing a power system, we wanted to separate our high power systems
from our sensing and controls suite for noise and safety reasons. Our high power safety
shutoff is 36V volt contactor that is controlled by a relay. To power our lower voltage
electronics, we use a 14S power conversion module. Using a 14S power module gives us
a significant factor of safety to handle power spikes, something we needed as last year we
blew a 10S power conversion module. The power diagram for the vehicle can be seen
below (Figure 19).
11Figure 19: High power systems and power conversion. Note that the nominal voltage of the system is 28.8V,
but it gets as high as 33V on full charge
For propulsion and steering, we use the aforementioned ZTW Seal 300A ESC and
Leopard 56110 on our 28.8V line, and we run our steering servos with 8.4V. They give
70kg of torque each and are waterproof, providing sufficient reliability (Figure 21).
Figure 20: Our propulsion and steering powertrain
Payload
With the introduction of a variable payload into this year’s competition, many
design decisions were made to adapt to this new format. To be as competitively viable as
possible, it was decided to make a payload flexible hull design for a pretty simple reason:
it gave the team the most paths to victory. In the event that the competition was filled
with fast, but light, 30lb payload boats, we could go light to keep pace with them. On the
other hand, if there is one exceptionally fast 30lb boat, but the rest are much slower, a
middling-speed 60lb payload boat can use its 5 point bonus to overtake the first place
team with a second place run time. As for our actual payload, we used steel shot balls in
shooting bags as they were maulable and adjustable to our needs (Figure 21).
Figure 21: Our payload bags (left) and our payload paths to the podium (right)
12Control System
Figure 22: The control and communications signals
The control system of the craft consists of a Pixhawk controller, a common flight
controller for RC drones and aircraft. We use the ArduRover firmware to configure our
pixhawk for use on Usain Boat. The flight controller has a built-in IMU. With an additional
GPS and current sensor we are able to monitor key facets of our craft. A Dragonlink RC
two-way radio system is used to control the vessel, and transmit telemetry data, such as
GPS location, current speed, and battery current draw and voltage to the pilot (Figure 22).
Figure 23: The Dragonlink RC Radio and Taranis controller
The Dragonlink system boasts a 50 km range, far more than is needed for the 2
mile race. For its price point, it is potentially the strongest commercial radio on the market
(Figure 23). Since the boat sits low in the water, there are concerns about Fresnel Zone
clearance. To alleviate that concern, Usain Boat’s receiver antenna is high up on the boat.
This combined with the strength of the transmitter provides a reliable solution against
obstructions and allows confidence in the performance of the craft’s radio.
Figure 24: The CAD and resulting 3D print of one of the rudders
13Since Usain Boat is equipped with only a single propeller, a separate rudder system
was created to steer the craft. This system adds a rudder on either side of the propeller
and these rudders are attached to servos that can be controlled with our Taranis controller
over a Dragonlink radio connection to turn the vehicle. The rudders were designed in
Solidworks, then 3D printed before being attached to our boat (Figure 24).
Risk
When designing a Usain Boat, it was important to take into account the risks
associated with the different parts of the craft. Usain Boat only has a singular propeller,
which poses complications in terms of turning the vehicle, ensuring there is enough
power from the singular propeller to drive the boat forward with a 30-60 pound payload,
and presents the risk of not having any propulsion should the propeller fail. In order to
account for these risks, proper protocols and additions to the craft have been put into
place. To handle the issue of steering a rudder system has been attached to the back of
the craft, allowing it to turn. Our team also makes sure to keep the propeller clear, both to
keep themselves safe and not cause damage to the propeller. There was also proper
research done to ensure the motor met the required specifications to provide the
propeller with enough power to move the craft, even while operating with a payload.
The motor of Usain Boat is connected to the propeller using a flexible shaft. This
flexible shaft is susceptible to unwinding if mishandled, so care is always taken whenever
attaching the motor and the propeller or when working with the shaft. In addition to this,
care and proper precautions are taken when working with the batteries that provide
power to the vehicle. The boat operates on Lithium ion batteries, which are safer than
LiPo batteries, but still pose risks. When the batteries are not in use, they are stored in a
flammables bag or in a flammables cabinet (Figure 25), and it is ensured that they are
charged properly to avoid damaging the batteries and increasing their risk of harm. There
is also always sand available in our lab space, in case a fire were to occur.
Figure 25: Lithium Ion Battery Bag Figure 26: Contactor Kill Switch
The team works with fiberglass and epoxy often, using them to fabricate the hull of
the vehicle, and can be exposed to harmful chemicals when working with these materials
as well as when participating in activities such as foam cutting. In order to minimize the
risk when working with these materials, it is ensured that proper protective equipment,
including gloves, masks, goggles, and respirators are worn. It is also ensured that these
materials are utilized correctly and safely. For example, we made sure that there was no
loose fiberglass on the hull of the boat and that all of the epoxy had cured correctly.
To account for any risks that could occur during the race, the craft has a contactor
kill switch installed, in addition to a physical kill switch, that allows Usain Boat to be shut
down remotely (Figure 26). That means if any issue is to occur during the race, the vehicle
can quickly and safely be shut down to minimize any potential hazards.
14Conclusion
Usain Boat is the result of well over 1000 hours of work from our dedicated team at
NUWave. It’s designed to be a “bulletproof boat,” capable of running reliably even in
adverse circumstances. It is equipped to operate at either the 30lb or 60lb payload
weight in order to optimize to competition circumstances, and it features an entirely new
propulsion system from last year’s design. It boasts a wide variety of safety features from
contactors to waterproof hatches to create a secure craft.
When considering future directions, the team is considering adding a second
propeller to both double the thrust and replace the rudder with a differential thrust
turning system for sharper corners. Our software system also enables improvement
through autonomy strategies like waypoint following and raceline optimization.
